diagnostic_item.correct_answer: No — the parts must be equal size for 1/4 to be correct

distractors.value: Yes, 1/4, because 1 out of 4 parts is shaded

diagnostic_item.stem: A square is cut into 4 parts of clearly different sizes and 1 part is shaded. Is the shaded part 1/4 of the square?

intervention.script: Watch me fold the paper in half twice to make four TRULY equal parts — now every piece matches.

labels.evidence_span: the parts have to be the same size

learner_evidence.explanation: no, because the parts have to be the same size to call it 1/4, these pieces are all different sizes

caveats: transfer confirmed on a number line only; set-model transfer not yet attempted
mastery_outcome.claim: Ava can judge whether a partition shows equal parts before naming a fraction

misconception.citation: Research on children's partitioning strategies and the equal-parts requirement in early fraction instruction.
misconception.cognitive_origin: Children over-attend to the COUNT of pieces and under-attend to their SIZE, so any shape divided into N regions is labeled '1/N' regardless of whether the regions are equal — a failure to encode equal partitioning as a defining feature of a fraction.
misconception.title: Unequal partitions still count as a valid fraction

sprout_scripts.utterance: I cut it into 4 pieces, so each piece is 1/4 — the sizes don't matter!
Does it matter if the pieces are different sizes, as long as there are 4?
